extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; people learning heuristics for solving mathematical problems
extracted.subtask_description: Practical heuristics and diagnostic criteria for inventing, executing, and checking solutions to mathematical (and analogous) problems; guidance for teachers diagnosing student faults. Emphasizes definitions, diagrams, use of data, related problems, generalization, and perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going back to definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Going back to definitions is important in inventing an argument but it is also important in checking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for the moment when the solver uses the definition or a theorem about the object (example: sphere/Archimedes). If such a moment never comes, the solution is no good. When checking your own argument ask: Have you taken into account all essential notions? How did you use this notion — its meaning or its definition? (See Pascal: “Substituer mentalement les définitions à la place des définis.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the meanings behind words and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek meaning and facts behind the words; words and signs have power because of the ideas and facts they recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on mere verbal sound or 'hot air'; treat words as reminders of concrete relations and facts. Mathematicians should get hold of actual relations behind technical terms, analogous to physicists checking experiments behind terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and proportionate determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination, hope, and success matter: solving serious problems requires will power that can outlast long toil and disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportion determination to outlook: start only if the problem has some interest; settle to work if the problem seems instructive; seek small successes first (if you cannot solve the proposed problem, try a related problem). Beware of lukewarm effort for serious problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher’s role: stimulate curiosity and allow time
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher wishing to help should first stir up the student's curiosity and give time to make up his mind and settle to the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching to solve problems is education of the will; provide problems that are not too easy so students learn to persevere through failure and appreciate small advances and waiting for the essential idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis of student work (closer characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnose students’ work to characterize good and bad points more closely than a crude grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagnosis to identify specific faults in the phases of solution (understanding, planning, carrying out, checking) so the teacher can prescribe remedies—analogous to a physician diagnosing a patient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to the four phases of a solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish and monitor the phases: understanding the problem, devising a plan, carrying out the plan, and checking the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student behaviour is characteristic in each phase; use phase-specific questions and interventions. Typical faults cluster by phase (e.g., incomplete understanding, lack of plan, carelessness in execution, failure to check result).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure complete understanding of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete understanding due to lack of concentration is a widespread deficiency; ensure you understand what the unknown, data, and condition are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Did you use all the data? Is your conception adequate? For 'problems to prove': Did you use the whole hypothesis? Example: parallelepiped problem where a student omitted datum c — teacher can prompt to bring c into play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all parts of the hypothesis / data
rubrics_metrics.description: For perfectly stated theorems/problems each clause of the hypothesis is essential; neglecting any part usually makes a proof wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking a proof ask where each part of the hypothesis is used. For problems 'perfectly stated and reasonable' you must use all the data and the whole condition. For practical problems (not perfectly stated) be prepared to reconsider the formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid two contrasting planning faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Two opposite faults in devising a plan: rushing into calculations without any plan, or waiting clumsily for some idea while doing nothing useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you rush, you may perform irrelevant calculations; if you idle, you lose time. Encourage active attempts to devise a plan: try related problems, simplify, or introduce auxiliary elements to stimulate ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out plans carefully and check each step
rubrics_metrics.description: The most frequent fault in carrying out the plan is carelessness and lack of patience in checking each step; failure to check results is very frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be satisfied simply to obtain an answer; inspect intermediate steps, verify reasonableness of results, and be shocked by unlikely answers. Teach students to check and to validate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a checklist of diagnostic questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use targeted questions to construct or check a solution: Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition? Have you taken into account all essential notions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions help find missing elements and show where conception is weak. They supply a line of inquiry and can point toward the decisive idea (examples and cross-references: DEFINITION, AUXILIARY ELEMENTS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check possibility and reasonableness of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Before assuming a problem is well posed, ask: Is it possible to satisfy the condition? Is the problem reasonable and perfectly stated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems in textbooks are usually perfectly stated but practical problems often are not; when in doubt ask whether the condition can be satisfied or whether some hypotheses are redundant or contradictory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use related problems (generalization/specialization/analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for formerly solved problems related to the present problem — by generalization, specialization, or analogy — and try to use their results or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobilize previously acquired knowledge and theorems. Example: using construction methods for circumscribed circle of a triangle to approach the circumscribed sphere of a tetrahedron by introducing analogous perpendicular bisecting planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary elements to make use of related problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When trying to use a formerly solved problem, consider introducing auxiliary elements so that its result or method becomes applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in the tetrahedron example, introducing perpendicular bisecting planes mirrors the triangle case. Ask: Could you use its result? Could you use its method? Should you introduce some auxiliary element to make its use possible?

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and test guesses critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept vivid guesses as proven truths; examine guesses that arise after attentive consideration — they often contain fragments of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn promising guesses into 'problems to prove' by formulating them precisely. Examples: guessing the square as the quadrilateral with greatest area, then restating as a theorem to prove; the John Jones anti-pattern where unchecked suspicions become dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform 'problem to find' into 'problem to prove' by formulating guesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate an attractive guess precisely to convert a 'find' problem into a 'prove' problem and then attempt to prove or disprove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This often clarifies the goal and makes the problem more tractable (example: guess that the square maximizes area among quadrilaterals with fixed perimeter, then restate and prove a weaker related statement such as among rectangles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures, diagrams and geometric representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw figures to represent the unknown and the data; figures help assemble and retain details and often simplify reasoning even for non-geometric problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to imagine or draw; for many details a paper figure is indispensable. Figures help separate and recombine details, suggest auxiliary elements, and provide a basis for constructing and checking solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for drawing figures (exactness, avoiding specialization, notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether figures should be exact or approximate; avoid figures that suggest undue special cases; use notation and line styles to clarify roles of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners should construct exact figures to acquire experimental basis, but free-hand figures are usually sufficient for reasoning. Avoid drawings that imply equalities or special properties not required by the problem. Use heavy/light or dotted lines, colors, and light lines for tentative auxiliaries; draw general shapes (e.g., a 45°/60°/75° triangle) to avoid special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hypothetical/constructive assumption technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin solving construction problems by drawing a hypothetical figure that assumes the desired condition is already satisfied (Pappus: 'Assume what is required to be done as already done').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique applies beyond construction problems: examine the hypothetical situation in which the problem condition is fully satisfied to guide discovery of auxiliary elements and relations. Do not confuse possibility with certainty; postpone judgment until examination yields definite results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize problem statements (replace numbers by letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing from specific numerical instances to a more general statement (numbers→letters) can reveal methods and enable checks and variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization may make the problem easier (Inventor’s paradox). It affords new procedures, allows parameter variation to test results, and sometimes simplifies by revealing essential structure (examples: sums of cubes forming squares; frustum volume in letters a,b,h).
